note:
v1, EXTREME AND MEAN: THE SEVENTH SONG, A SKELETON (Harry, 17 Nov about 03:40: "open up 2 new song slots"). The record's slow song: 80, where the other six run 100 to 138.
The riff is two cells, a long (three sixteenths) and a short (two), and one rule: every long becomes a long and a short, every short becomes a long. Apply it again and again and you get a pattern of longs and shorts that never falls into a loop, yet every stretch of it comes back, and it is the same at every size. So the band plays the one pattern at many sizes at once: the guitars' muted strokes are the smallest cells; where a cell of eight or five sixteenths begins the string is let ring; where one of thirteen or eight begins there is a chord; where one of thirty-four or twenty-one begins, a crash; and the song's own eight sections go long, short, long, long, short, long, short, long: the long ones heavy, the short ones quiet. The form is the riff, 78 times slower. The kit keeps common time against all of it and starts its count again with each section.
In the quiet sections a wire harp (new on this record) has no written notes: the engine is given the same rule and plays it, each short cell a step higher than the long one that made it. In the last section the harp plays over the band.
The title is Euclid's phrase for a line cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter. Such a cut has no common measure; neither has this riff.
WHERE THINGS ARE: heavy 0:00, quiet 0:44, heavy 1:11, heavy on A flat with four guitars 1:54, quiet 2:38, heavy 3:05, quiet 3:49, heavy with the harp 4:16, one chord 4:59.

- It is slow, not sparse: the scorer counts 6.0 onsets a second, as on the other six.

v2, THE SAME TUNE AT EVERY SIZE (a whole-song round, taken openly: the draw was Odd Sympathy, which I passed; v1's note said the three quiet sections were the same nine bars three times).
The song's idea is one pattern at every size, and the band already plays it so in the heavy sections. Now the harps do too. The first quiet section is as it was: one harp, the tune on the smallest cells (three and two sixteenths). In the second there are two harps: the new one plays THE SAME TUNE on the next size of cell (five and three sixteenths), an octave lower. In the third there are three: the third plays it on cells of eight and five, an octave lower again. It is a canon in which nobody starts late: the voices start together and go at different speeds, and the speeds stand to each other as the long cell to the short. Because the larger cells are made of the smaller, every note of a slower harp falls exactly with a note of the faster ones.
The engine plays all of it from the one rule; no harp has a written note.

note: CORRECTION to v2's note (chirper-zero): I wrote that my first levels were wrong because 'the lower harps ring longer'. I did not measure that. What I measured: I had set the lower harps 1 and 2 dB HIGHER than the first harp, guessing they would read weaker, and they read 0.7 and 2.7 dB over it. So at equal gain the harp an octave down is about level with the first (0.3 under) and the one two octaves down about 0.7 over. The mistake was my guess, not the string. The rest stands.

v3, BREATH FOR THE LARGEST SIZE (a palette round, as drawn: the part the song lacked, on a sound no other song has).
The band plays the one pattern at many sizes, but one size had no voice of its own: cells of 21 and 13 sixteenths, about four seconds and two and a half. That is as long as a note can usefully be held, so it is where a tune can be sung slowly. In the three four-guitar sections (1:54, 3:05, 4:16) a brass section, horns and trombones, now plays the harp's tune on those cells, one long note to a cell. Strings are plucked for the small sizes; breath holds the large one. It is the same tune again (the canon of v2 went down three sizes in the quiet sections; this is a fourth, in the heavy ones).
The brass is the engine's physical model of lips on a tube, the first wind instrument on the record.

WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether at this level the brass is heard as a voice or only felt as thickness (the flag takes any level: say "louder" and it is one number); whether horns under distorted guitars sound grand or like a film trailer; whether, with the harp also on top, the last section is too full.

v4, THE SHORT LINE IS THE HEAD OF THE LONG ONE (palette). For the end of the second two-guitar riff only, a dry pedal steel slides through four notes and repeats just the first three. Its phrases last 55 then 34 sixteenths; the short copy breaks off before the fill. The first F bends to Ab while the fretted guitars keep chopping underneath it. No change to their notes, to the brass, or to the final section. C10T7_STEEL='' regenerates v3 byte for byte.
